volume.source: China Global South Project / OilPrice.com reporting on Saudi-China crude flows

explainer: China is Saudi Arabia's largest single oil customer by far. If this flow were cut, Saudi Arabia would need to find other Asian buyers at a discount, and China would need to replace its single largest crude supplier.

volume.source: The Arabian Stories, citing Omani customs data

explainer: Oman sells almost all its oil to one buyer. That concentration is a risk for Oman, but the flow itself is largely insulated from a Hormuz shock, since Oman's export terminals sit on the Gulf of Oman, outside the strait.

volume.source: Reuters, via The Moscow Times and United24 Media (TurkStream data)

explainer: This flow has collapsed from 152.4 bcm in 2021 to a fraction of that since the EU deliberately diversified away from it. The remaining volume runs through a single route, TurkStream, into Hungary, Slovakia and Serbia.

volume.source: Gazprom data, via MarketScreener and World-Energy

explainer: As Russia's gas sales to Europe collapsed, China became its substitute buyer. The Power of Siberia pipeline has little spare capacity left, which is why Russia and China are now discussing a second, larger line.

volume.source: S&P Global Commodity Insights, citing South Korean import data (19.5% of Korea's total LNG imports)

explainer: South Korea leans on Qatar for roughly a fifth of its LNG imports. A Hormuz disruption threatens this flow directly, since Qatari LNG has no bypass route around the strait.

volume.source: S&P Global Commodity Insights, one month's Japanese import data (5.4% of Japan's total LNG imports that month)

explainer: A smaller but steady flow. Japan diversifies its LNG suppliers more than South Korea does, so a Qatari disruption would be a squeeze rather than a crisis for Japan specifically.

volume.source: Iraqi News, citing Iraqi oil ministry data

explainer: Iraq's one real bypass route around Hormuz, agreed with Turkey in August 2026. It covers a small fraction of Iraq's total exports, most of which still move through the Gulf.

volume.source: Tehran Times and OilPrice.com, down from a contracted 50 mcm/day under US sanctions pressure

explainer: Iraq depends on Iranian gas to keep its power plants running, but US sanctions pressure has repeatedly cut this flow well below what was contracted, forcing recurring electricity shortages.
Once Saudi Arabia's top customer, the US now takes a small share of its exports after the shale revolution made America a net oil exporter in its own right.
India's fast-growing economy makes it an increasingly important buyer of Saudi crude, competing with China for supply.
India is one of the UAE's largest oil customers, part of a broader trade relationship that also includes gold and other goods.
Japan has bought UAE crude for decades under long-term supply agreements, part of why Japan has pushed the UAE and Saudi Arabia on new Hormuz-bypass pipeline capacity.
China buys more Qatari LNG than any other country, under long-term contracts that give Qatar unusually stable, locked-in revenue.
Qatar is India's single largest LNG supplier. A sustained Hormuz disruption would force India to compete harder for cargoes from the US, Australia or elsewhere.

Once a major LNG supplier to Europe, Egypt's exports have shrunk as rising domestic demand turned it into a net gas importer by 2024, a reminder that export flows can disappear from the demand side, not just the supply side.
China is a major buyer of Kuwaiti crude, but unlike Oman, Kuwait's entire export route runs through the Gulf and the strait, with no bypass pipeline of its own.
China is Iraq's largest single oil customer, buying around a third of its crude exports.
India is Iraq's second-largest crude buyer. Both of Iraq's top two customers depend on oil that has to cross the Strait of Hormuz to reach them.
